doc.title: John Bunch interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Jazz education and Mike LeDonne
summary: Bunch doubts he can teach; he recalls Mike LeDonne and says records are how you learn.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: The way that you’ve learned, you’ve played with a lot of great musicians, is jazz education different now? And is it better or is it missing something?

Well see you’re asking the wrong guy. I don’t know anything about jazz education. I don’t even understand how there could be such a term as jazz education. But I know it’s going on. In fact the very university, Indiana University where I went to school, and I

said they frowned on jazz. Well now it’s known as one of the best schools I guess in the country to teach jazz. And so I mean never having, no one’s ever asked me to you know, lecture or say anything in front of young students, so I just wouldn’t know much about that. I guess there are ways of teaching it but I don’t know how it’s done really. Ignorant about that. You know one pianist, by the way, when he was about eighteen years old, kept hanging around me trying to get me to teach, you know give him lessons. And I told him I wouldn’t know how to teach and you have to want to do that. You have to have desire for that. And he finally talked me into coming, I said, alright, come up to my apartment and I want to hear you play. This guy came up there and played so much more piano than I do — it was embarrassing. His name was Mike LeDonne. Have you ever heard of him? Boy he’s really great. He’s becoming a hell of a piano player. He’s playing with people like Milt Jackson quite a lot. He’s playing with Sonny Rollins lately too. So I mean I told him, you’re already playing with guys that I wanted to play with all my life and never got a chance to you know, really. So it was — I just felt like there was nothing I could show him you know. Maybe I’m putting myself down when I say that. Maybe there is something. I don’t know what it would be though. I think that a young person, if they have a lot of talent, records are very important. Scott Hamilton’s got a record collection you wouldn’t believe. He knows much more about saxophone players than I do. He’s put together some tapes for me that are wonderful stuff that I never even knew existed, you know like — so I’m saying that he learned a lot from listening to records. He lived in, up there in a small town outside of Providence, Rhode Island you know and like I lived in this very small farm town. But the records, you know I started hearing these records. And if you’ve got really the talent, you know you can steal from these guys. Steal whatever you can. It’s fun when you’re a kid it’s really fun to try to play like them you know. And I think that’s how you learn.
